title: Fires, Tornado And Many Changes Recalled By 78-Year-Old Savoy
text:
GOLD NUGGETS BOUGHT LAND

Fires, Tornado And Many Changes
Recalled By 78-Year-Old Savoy

By ELIZABETH LARGE

SAVOY — Approximately 100 residents in this Fannin community observed the 78th birth-day of their city. Officers Marshal Lewis Holland Son and daughter-in-law Mr. and Mrs. Marshall Savoy will be buried in California '49. Contributing [illegible] Dr. Col. Savoy[?] and Bear, M.T. Best opened the business district. D. G. Atteberry[?] [illegible] road in 1949 and his first general[?] store

HIT BY CYCLONE

In January 1949[?], the entire business section was destroyed by a cyclone. Thirteen were killed. Twelve were killed and the old Halsell College was turned into an emergency hospital.

The businesses had a lot of wood construction. In later years there was no interruption in the water. The business district was moved to Hayes Street where it remains today.

Last of the old buildings to be used for businesses were those owned by the late W.L. Teague. A store behind the D. G. Atteberry building.

D. Atteberry Dry Goods Store is the oldest business in Savoy. It was established in 1869 by its founder, son of its founder, his son and daughter-in-law Mr. and Mrs. [illegible]. The Lackey[?] building[?] is still[?] an outpost[?].

[?] in Mississippi and died Sept. 1 in California. Col. Savoy came to Texas at an early age settling in Grayson County. He spent his latter[?] years at the Savoy Plantation. He was a colonel in the [illegible] and served time in the Confederate Army but never [illegible] a rank higher than Lieutenant Colonel.

Second generation, when the years were spent traveling. The Savoys spent the Atlantic[?] [illegible] to the Pacific three times. It is believed by his daughter, Mrs. Ada Savoy Travis that he was doing secret service work for the government at this time.

He joined the Gold Rush and sometime. While there he dug[?] gold[?] nuggets[?] while[?] his partner[?] a heavy cotton bag later buying the land on which Savoy was founded with part of it.

D. Atteberry, dry goods; D. T. Jarvis, lumber; Lovall [?] & Sons[?], hardware; D. G. Atteberry, groceries and confections; John Large, groceries; D. M. Harp[?]; barber; McMahon, Durrell & Co., drugs; Nelson Hodges, black-smith; W. L. Teague, groceries and confections; E. A. Harp, groceries; T. Buffalo, groceries; P. M. Denger[?], drugs; D. C. McKinnon, hardware and drugs.

JOINED GOLD RUSH

In 1949 he joined in the gold rush in California and came home to water. While there he dug gold nuggets while his partner filled a heavy cotton bag later buying the land on which Savoy was founded with part of it.

A first light plant was owned and operated by the late D. G. Atteberry. Most of the houses had electricity, and the business houses were also equipped with the same.

In 1913 Sam Baker, now of Dallas, took over the plant. He operated it until 1913 when he sold it. Baker retained the plant and he solved the water problem. The water supply was a surface lake water to the city.

Holligan[?], a graduate of Abilene Christian College, has been in Savoy for 16 months. He has been carrying the mail for about 40 years. He died there in 1924. The electric light system was owned by the late Tom Frank[?].

EARLY POSTMASTERS

Savoy's first postmaster in 1884 was young Person[?] [illegible]; and his name was something between him[?] and theirs[?] [illegible] W.P. [illegible], who had been a resident between 10 and 12 years and had served for 12 years[?] and returned[?] to [illegible] a second resident[?]. Claud Strickland was appointed in 1942 Carter in March, 1941.[?] The present[?] postmaster[?] is Claud Strickland. The rural carrier out of Savoy who can be recalled is A. [illegible]. McMahon, now of Dallas; Will McSpadden, now of Durant, Okla.; Will D. G. Franks, carrier in Denison at the time of his death, served together for many years. Lester Hinaley[?] of Van Alstyne came to Savoy in 1958 and has been carrying the mail for two years. At this time Savoy has four churches today; Baptist; Methodist; Church of Christ; and Church of[?] [illegible]; the Rev. W. A. Lindauer, Baptist; the Rev. W. [illegible], Earl[?] Napp, pastor; and Pentecost[?] [illegible] Rev. A. H. [illegible].

Present Savoy businesses: Savoy Grocery[?]; George Blakey's filling station; Cecil Moore, hardware and drugs; Robinson[?] Grocery[?]; George Waldrum[?] Auto[?]; Post Office operated by Jim Reynolds; blacksmith; Bradshaw's[?] filing station; Karl Blakey's filing station; Jim Waldrum's garage; [illegible].

H. F. Bomar, Gr[?] Grocer[?]; Jim Orr, Bro.; Grocer[?]; Jack Waldrum, hardware and drugs; B. C. Doan, radio repair; Waldrum[?] Barber shop; Kelso and Waldrum, battery shop; and Charles Strickland, postmaster and funeral director.
notes: Article is significantly damaged/degraded and many portions are illegible or uncertain. The article appears to commemorate Savoy's 78th anniversary (suggesting a date around 1954-1955 if founding was 1876-1878). The 'cyclone' destroying the entire business section with '13 killed' and Halsell College used as emergency hospital aligns with the 1896 or another known storm. Multiple sections are fragmentary. Byline is Elizabeth Large, Savoy correspondent. The 'GOLD NUGGETS BOUGHT LAND' headline appears as a sub-section head. The 'JOINED GOLD RUSH' section appears to repeat content with slight variation — this may be a printing artifact or pagination issue in the original. Many names and dates marked [?] due to image degradation. The list of early and present businesses is partially legible.
